text: What is GSE309890 about, and what files can I actually download?

## Abstract (168 words)  
In this investigation, we queried the public GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) database to determine the details of the study GSE309890 and identify which files are available for download. GSE309890 reports on an Escherichia coli strain K-12 MG1655 study that examines how the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor sertraline promotes the emergence of resistance to specific antibiotics via metabolic rewiring in the pentose phosphate pathway. Using the “geo_series” tool, we entered the Series accession GSE309890 with the option “list_files” to retrieve metadata and supplementary file information. The return included one CSV file containing gene expression data (510 KB, compressed) from an RNA-seq experiment involving six samples across different experimental conditions. The accompanying publication date is 2026/02/01, and we confirmed there is no currently listed PubMed reference for this study in the GEO record. The supplementary file directory hosting the data is accessible through the GEO FTP site. This metadata and file availability enable researchers to analyze expression profiling results for antibiotic resistance under SSRI treatment pressure.

## I. Introduction  
### Background  
GSE309890 is a GEO Series record that investigates how sertraline, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), influences antibiotic resistance in E. coli. SSRIs are widely used in human medicine to treat depression, but there is concern that they may inadvertently drive antibiotic resistance.  

### Literature Review  
No literature was retrieved for this query.  

### Knowledge Gap  
It was unclear how sertraline reshapes metabolic pathways within E. coli to alter susceptibility patterns to commonly used antibiotics.  

### Objective & Hypothesis  
The objective was to understand the mechanisms by which sertraline promotes antibiotic resistance in E. coli. The study hypothesized that sertraline could trigger specific metabolic shifts—especially in the pentose phosphate pathway—that confer reduced susceptibility or promote resistance through alteration of cellular redox mechanisms.  

## II. Materials and Methods  
### Study Design  
We performed a targeted database query to identify GEO Series record GSE309890, focusing on the record’s title, summary, and available files.  

### Materials  
• Database: GEO (via geo_series)  

### Procedures  
1. geo_series(accession=“GSE309890”, list_files=true) – called with accession = GSE309890 to retrieve the summary of the study and details of downloadable files.  

### Statistical Analysis  
No numerical summarization was required apart from listing the total number of samples and supplementary data file(s).  

## III. Results

### Findings  
• GSE309890 studies the influence of sertraline on antibiotic resistance in E. coli.  
• Six samples are listed.  
• One supplementary file is available, which appears to contain FPKM data for all samples.  

## IV. Discussion  
### Interpretation  
The retrieved metadata indicates that this study focuses on a significant research question: understanding how SSRIs, specifically sertraline, shape bacterial metabolic pathways to alter antibiotic susceptibility. The presence of a single CSV file suggesting FPKM-based gene expression information indicates that the authors extensively characterized transcriptomic responses in E. coli.  

### Context  
The data are hosted in GEO as a Series record (GSE309890). No literature references are directly associated with this GEO accession, suggesting potential further analysis or ongoing publication efforts.  

### Limitations  
• The record does not yet have an associated PubMed entry in GEO, signalling that it may be currently unpublished or awaiting indexing.  
• The study’s complete raw data for expression is available only via the supplementary file in CSV format on the GEO FTP server.  

### Conclusion & Future Directions  
Our findings show that GSE309890 centers on sertraline-induced antibiotic resistance. Researchers can access the data by downloading the single CSV file provided in the supplementary directory. Future directions might include further analysis of the metabolic changes involved and expanding literature searches to capture forthcoming publications related to this dataset.

## Acknowledgments  
We thank the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) for providing the GEO Series record and supplementary files.
